John Norton
jon nôr'tən
n. (John Norton, 1606–1663, teacher of the First Church in Boston, author of The Orthodox Evangelist)
English surname Norton, from the north farmstead or settlement.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

John Norton came to New England in 1635, served Ipswich with Nathaniel Ward, and succeeded John Cotton as teacher of the First Church in Boston. He was the colony's chief controversialist. His The Orthodox Evangelist (1654) is a systematic treatment of the person of Christ, the covenant, and effectual calling; he answered William Pynchon's book denying that Christ suffered the penal wrath of God, and his Discussion of the Great Point in Divinity, the Sufferings of Christ is a defence of penal substitution against the view that the atonement was a transaction of obedience only. He wrote the first American life of a minister, of Cotton, and in 1662 went with Simon Bradstreet as the colony's agent to Charles II. He also wrote in defence of the capital laws against the Quakers, under which four were hanged. Gal 1:8 is the text he applied freely, and 1Jn 4:1 the duty he discharged.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines orthodox as sound in the Christian faith, and substitution as the act of putting one person or thing in the place of another.

expand to see more

OR'THODOX, a. Sound in the Christian faith; believing the genuine doctrines taught in the Scriptures; opposed to heretical.

SUBSTITU'TION, n. The act of placing one person or thing in the place of another, to supply its want.

SAT'ISFACTION, n. That which satisfies; amends; atonement; payment; indemnification for an injury.

Key Scripture

Gal 1:8 — "But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed."

1Jn 4:1 — "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world."

Tit 1:11 — "Whose mouths must be stopped, who subvert whole houses, teaching things which they ought not, for filthy lucre's sake."

Act 20:30 — "Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them."

Modern Corruption

He defended penal substitution ably and defended the gallows for Quakers, and the dictionary separates the two.

expand to see more

Norton's answer to Pynchon is the valuable half of him. Pynchon had argued that Christ did not bear the Father's penal wrath but offered a perfect obedience which God accepted; Norton showed that this empties the satisfaction of its content, since a penalty not borne is a penalty remitted without payment. The dictionary holds substitutionary penal atonement, and Norton's treatise is one of the earliest American defences of it. 1Jn 4:1 commands the trying of spirits and Gal 1:8 supplies the seriousness of the verdict where another gospel is in view.

His defence of the capital laws against the Quakers must be named as the error it was, and naming it is not a concession to modern sentiment but an application of the same Scripture. The magistrate's sword in Rom 13:4 is for evildoers in the civil order; a man's return to a colony that has banished him for his religion is not a crime against person or property. Four Quakers were hanged in Boston between 1659 and 1661, and the colony later repented of it. Tit 1:11 says of false teachers that their “mouths must be stopped” (Tit 1:11) — stopped by sound doctrine, which is the instrument Paul names in the same chapter, not by execution.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek anathema (G331), accursed; dokimazo (G1381), to try; epistomizo (G1993), to stop the mouth.

expand to see more

Greek anathema (G331) — accursed, devoted to destruction; Galatians 1:8.

Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to try, prove; 1 John 4:1.

Greek epistomizo (G1993) — to stop the mouth, silence; Titus 1:11.

Greek anatrepo (G396) — to overthrow, subvert; Titus 1:11.

Greek diastrepho (G1294) — to pervert; Acts 20:30.

Usage

"“let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8) — the verdict on another gospel."

"“try the spirits whether they are of God” (1Jn 4:1) — the duty he discharged well."

"“Whose mouths must be stopped” (Tit 1:11) — by doctrine, not by the gallows."
